title: What is known about 1RB0LE_0LC0RA_1LE0RD_0RB---_0LF0LD_1LA0LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_0LC0RA_1LE0RD_0RB---_0LF0LD_1LA0LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state machine halts from blank tape. Its tape is single 1s separated by gaps of one, two or three 0s, and it grows to the left. At its visits to the left end a prefix made of the word 0 0 1 grows by one word each time while the time between visits roughly doubles, then shrinks back: the behavior of a counter. This page lists what has been established, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Its events are decoded: a binary counter at the left end (3-cell digits) gains 1 per event and a 2-bit counter M right of a fixed 46-cell word gains 1; this is proved in Lean for every carry length. When M wraps, a slower counter further right changes (not decoded), and now and then the fixed words themselves are rebuilt.

New, 14 November 2026. The whole run is now one rule: the tape is a binary counter with doublers (words 1010, 000, 100), and each round sends one defect through it. A tape with one defect cannot halt; a halt needs two defects to meet. In 100,000 rounds there was no halt, and in the 4,500 rounds followed word by word every defect disappeared long before the next one started. Whether that is always so is the open question.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 275 cells have been visited and 85 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Sweep rules
claims.text: A, B, C and D cross runs of the words 01, 10, 001 or 100 rightwards in one state, rewriting each copy the same way, for any number of copies and any surrounding tape.

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator runs 10<sup>9</sup> steps without a halt.

claims.title: Visits to the left end
claims.text: At the visits of E to the left end on blank the tape is E>0 0 1 (0 0 1)^k 0 1 … followed by single 1s with gaps of one to three 0s. k grows by 1 from one visit to the next while the time between visits roughly doubles, and drops back now and then (to 8 at step 4,121,436; to 2 at step 109,450,476, after reaching 18).

claims.title: Where it can halt
claims.text: A closed tape language with windows of 6 cells (found and checked by bbtools.ctl, not yet in Lean) allows a halt only with D reading a 1 at the left end of the tape, followed by 100100, 100101, 101001 or 101010.

claims.title: A counter
claims.text: A word per visit and twice the time per word is the signature of a binary counter whose digits are the gaps; the drops of k are its carries reaching further into the tape.

claims.title: The rule
claims.text: How the gaps encode a number, and what a visit does to it, are not known.

claims.title: The event rule (non-wrapping events)
claims.text: From L 0 0 0 (1 0 0)^k ENGINE A> 0 PREFIX [M] R (ENGINE = 00101001010100, PREFIX the 46-cell word 1001010100100101010010001001000100100010101010, M two 4-cell digits 1000 = 0 / 1010 = 1, low first) the machine reaches the same shape with the left counter + 1 (1 0 0 (0 0 0)^k) and M + 1, for M = 0, 1, 2, every k and every tape L, R (8k + 608 or 8k + 616 steps); also when the k ones reach the left end of the tape (the counter gains a digit). Nothing right of M is read.

claims.title: Events in the run
claims.text: With this ENGINE and PREFIX, events run from step 78,415 (left counter 32, M = 1): 110 consecutive events add 1 to both counters (27 of them wraps of M), up to left counter 142; then the PREFIX is rebuilt (one of the drops of the left-end count noted above).

claims.title: The wrap of M and beyond
claims.text: When M wraps, a slower counter right of M (4-cell words 0101/0100 and others) changes; how, and how the PREFIX is rebuilt, is not decoded. A halt (D reading 1) can only come in those steps, never inside a non-wrapping event.

claims.title: The run as rounds of one function
claims.text: On the mirrored tape, a visit of A (the head at a cell in state A until it first steps left of it) is a function on the half tape, and four such functions (A, E, F, P) close up. From [A] 0 0 S the machine returns to [A] 0 0 S' one cell further out with S' = 1 0 A(S). Derived by local simulation and checked against direct simulation of the machine.

claims.title: No halt in 100,000 rounds
claims.text: The visit engine, with visit counts kept as sums of powers of two, ran 100,000 rounds without a halt; the counts reach 187,512 bits. Only 7 window rules of A and E are ever used.

claims.title: A counter with doublers and one travelling defect
claims.text: In the words L = 1010, O = 000, I = 100 the function A is a binary counter (O, I the digits) in which every carry crossing an L becomes two. Each round adds one defect (a 10, 1 or 0 that does not fit the words), which travels through the counter, rewrites it, and disappears where it turns 1 I O into O L. Worked out by hand from the four functions: a tape with one defect cannot halt; a halt needs two defects side by side. The token rules reproduce the exact tape cell for cell (rounds 5 to 24), and in every round from 13 to 4,500 the defect disappeared about 40% of the way into the tape, long before the round ended.

claims.title: Does every defect disappear in time?
claims.text: If the defect of every round disappears before the round ends, the machine never halts. Where it disappears depends on the digits of the counter, which look irregular; no proof.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. Its tape is single 1s with gaps of one to three 0s; read in 3-cell digits, the left end is a binary counter that gains 1 at every event, while a two-digit counter far to the right ticks along with it. That much is proved; what happens each time the small counter wraps is not yet decoded.

facts.text: The non-wrapping events for every carry length, in Lean.
Consecutive events of the proved shape (steps 78,415 on).

sections.heading: A counter with doublers and a travelling defect
html: Read the tape from right to left in the words L = 1010, O = 000, I = 100. A visit of state A to a tape of such words is a counter step:
A(O W) = I W   A(I W) = O A(W)   A(L W) = L A(A(W))

O and I are binary digits, lowest first, and L is a doubler: a carry that crosses it becomes two carries. One round of the machine is S' = 1 0 A(S). The 1 0 put in front does not fit the words; it is a defect. Pushed by the carries, the defect travels through the counter, rewrites the words it crosses, and disappears where it turns 1 I O into O L, two digits into a doubler. Every round adds exactly four words.

A tape with one defect cannot halt (worked out by hand from the rules, not yet in Lean). A halt needs two defects side by side, so the machine runs forever if every defect disappears before the next round starts. In every round from 13 to 4,500 it did, about 40% of the way into the tape; the run of 100,000 rounds (visit counts up to 187,512 bits) has no halt. Where the defect disappears depends on the digits of the counter, which look irregular: that is what a proof would have to control.

sections.heading: A binary counter at the left end
html: At an event the head is in state A just right of a fixed 14-cell word (the engine), and the tape reads

The left counter is binary with 3-cell digits 000 = 0 and 100 = 1, most significant first; M is two 4-cell digits 1000 = 0, 1010 = 1. One event: the head runs right through the 46-cell word (the head turns at several places inside it, rewriting and then restoring it: it comes back unchanged), adds 1 to M, returns, carries 1 into the left counter, and comes back: 608 + 8k steps for a carry over k ones. Example (steps 100,465, 101,089, 101,705, 102,321, 102,979): the left counter reads 1000011, 1000100, 1000101, 1000110, 1000111 and M = 0, 1, 2, 3, 0.

Proved in Lean for every k (lean/Events.lean). Open: what the wrap of M does to the slower counter further right, and the occasional rebuilding of the 46-cell word, which is when the count of the left-end visits drops.

sections.heading: Visits to the left end
html: Every so often the head reaches the left end of the tape in state E, on blank. The tape then starts E>0 0 1 (0 0 1)^k 0 1 … and continues with single 1s separated by one, two or three 0s. From step 109,450,476 on (run of 109 steps):

The gaps between visits are 14.5, 29.0, 57.9 million steps: they double, apart from some shorter ones where a carry stops early. Earlier the front went up to 14 (step 3,688,357), dropped to 8, went up to 11, dropped to 9, rose to 12, dropped to 11, and climbed to 18 (step 94,782,615) before dropping to 2.

sections.heading: Sweeps
html: The head crosses repeated words in one state, rewriting each copy the same way: for example A turns 0 1 into 1 0 and B turns 1 0 0 into 0 0 0. These rules are proved in Lean for any number of copies: a_right_01, a_right_001, b_right_10, b_right_100, c_right_10, d_right_01.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The machine halts only when D reads a 1. A closed tape language with windows of six cells (an over-approximation of the configurations reachable from blank tape, found by bbtools.ctl) allows that only at the left end of the tape, with 100100, 100101, 101001 or 101010 from the head on. Whether the counter ever leaves that pattern at the front when D arrives is the open question.

sections.heading: Next steps
html: Read the gaps as digits, write what one visit does to them and when the front collapses, and check the rule against the visits of a longer run; then find which value of the counter puts D on a 1 at the left end.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.08). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 275 cells (222 left of the start, 46 right), with a density of 1s of 0.309.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: Binary counter with doublers (words 1010, 000, 100) and one travelling defect per round; a tape with one defect cannot halt; no halt in 100,000 rounds; open: that every defect disappears before the next round.
